claims.text: Premelting and melting in HEA nanoparticles are governed by preferential surface segregation of lower-surface-energy elements.
The segregated elements form a liquid-like, disordered surface layer.
The disordered surface layer locally lowers the melting point well below the bulk value.
The proposed test system consists of equiatomic or near-equiatomic, sub-10 nm HEA nanoparticles prepared as homogeneous single-phase solid solutions on an inert substrate.
In situ TEM heating with sequential STEM imaging and EDS mapping can track structural and compositional changes from room temperature toward the bulk melting point.
Thermodynamic differences in elemental surface energies drive lower-surface-energy metals toward the nanoparticle surface.
Surface-energy differences cause faster diffusion of lower-surface-energy metals.
The segregated surface layer has a lower melting point than the well-mixed nanoparticle interior.
Formation of the segregated surface layer causes premelting before the rest of the nanoparticle reaches the bulk melting temperature.
Surface disorder and elemental enrichment will begin at a temperature significantly below the bulk melting point.
A surface treatment designed to suppress segregation will delay premelting relative to untreated nanoparticles.
If high-entropy stabilization remains uniform and prevents surface segregation, the nanoparticles will stay uniformly crystalline until the predicted bulk melting point.
Uniform high-entropy stabilization would produce no early surface premelting.
The proposed mechanism is expected to hold for sub-10 nm, equiatomic HEA nanoparticles with a narrow size distribution.
The governing mechanism may differ in larger nanoparticles or particles with preexisting compositional inhomogeneity.
Failure to detect either premelting surface segregation or a disordered liquid-like layer before bulk melting would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure of segregation-suppressing surface treatment to change the premelting onset temperature relative to untreated particles would falsify the hypothesis.
